lead: The first law of thermodynamics is an energy ledger. For a closed system, heat added minus work done equals the change in internal energy, and over a cycle net heat equals net work. The ledger always balances. It does not say which balanced process will happen. That gap matters when you judge a heat engine, a refrigerator, or a claim of a machine that turns all heat into work. This chapter lists what the first law cannot decide and names the law that fills the gap.
prereq: You need the energy balance from Chapter 2.1 and the losses in real devices from Chapter 2.6.

sections.h3: A balance sheet, not a compass

blocks.text: For a closed system the first law is Q − W = ΔU. Q is heat added to the system in kJ, W is work done by the system in kJ, and ΔU is the change in internal energy in kJ. For a complete cycle ΔU = 0, so Qnet = Wnet. Every joule is counted.

blocks.where: Q is heat added to the system in kJ; W is work done by the system in kJ; ΔU is the change in internal energy in kJ.

blocks.text: A cup of water at 80 °C in a room at 25 °C cools. Heat leaves the water and enters the room. The same number of joules can be written in the reverse direction: the room gives that heat back to the cup, and the cup warms to 80 °C. Both versions balance. Only the first happens on its own. The first law cannot choose between them.

This is the first limitation: no direction. A second limitation follows: no quality. A joule of work and a joule of heat are equal in energy units, but not equal in usefulness. Work can become heat completely through friction. In a cyclic engine, heat cannot become work completely; some heat must be rejected. The first law sees only totals, so it misses this difference.
Use these five limits as an exam checklist. Each is a job the first law cannot do.

items: No direction. Hot to cold and cold to hot both balance energy. The first law does not say which is spontaneous.
No quality. Work and heat are counted in the same unit, kJ. The first law does not mark work as more useful than heat.

It accepts a perpetual motion machine of the second kind, PMM-2. This is a device that takes heat from one reservoir and converts all of it into work in a cycle, with no cold reservoir. The first law gives Q = W, so it passes. The second law rejects it.
No criterion for equilibrium or spontaneity. It can balance a state that never occurs on its own.

No separation of reversible and irreversible processes. A slow reversible expansion and a fast irreversible one can have the same end states and the same energy balance, yet they differ in usefulness.

blocks.text: The first law also forbids a perpetual motion machine of the first kind, PMM-1, which creates energy. Do not mix the two. PMM-1 fails the first law. PMM-2 passes the first law and fails the second. See Chapter 2.5 for PMM-1.
The first law is still necessary. Any proposed process that fails the energy balance is impossible at once. The first law is a filter, not a full judge.

The missing rules come from the second law of thermodynamics. It states that heat flows on its own from hot to cold, and that a cyclic engine cannot convert all its heat input into work. Entropy gives a number for the direction. In an isolated system, the entropy of an irreversible process increases. The reverse of the cup cooling would decrease entropy, so it is forbidden even though energy balances.

The second law also separates quality. Work is high-grade energy. Heat at a low temperature is low-grade energy. Unit 3 develops the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements, the Carnot cycle and entropy. Unit 4 develops available energy, unavailable energy and exergy, which measure how much of an energy stream can become work.

For the cup in the worked example, cooling from 80 °C to 25 °C rejects 46.0 kJ. The reverse needs the room to give back exactly 46.0 kJ. Energy closes both ways. Only the second law rules out the reverse.

figure.caption: The first law balances heating and cooling with the same joules. It cannot pick the real direction, so the second law is needed.

spec.title: What the first law leaves open
spec.aria: The first law balances energy both ways round a process and so predicts no direction, which is why the second law is required.

examples.question: A cup holds 0.2 kg of water at 80 °C in a room at 25 °C. Take the specific heat of water as 4.18 kJ/kg·K. (a) Find the heat the water loses on cooling to room temperature. (b) Show that the reverse process also balances energy, and state which law rules it out.
steps: List data: m = 0.2 kg, c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K, T1 = 80 °C, T2 = 25 °C. The temperature drop is ΔT = 80 − 25 = 55 K.
0.2 × 4.18 = 0.836 kJ/K. Then 0.836 × 55 = 45.98 kJ, which rounds to 46.0 kJ.
The water rejects 46.0 kJ to the room.
For the reverse, the room supplies 46.0 kJ to the water. The water warms from 25 °C to 80 °C. The energy balance closes to the same 46.0 kJ.
The first law permits both directions. The second law forbids the reverse because it would reduce entropy.
examples.answer: The water loses 46.0 kJ on cooling; the reverse also balances at 46.0 kJ, and the second law rules it out.
examples.check:
m = 0.2
c = 4.18
T1 = 80.0
T2 = 25.0
Q = m * c * (T1 - T2)
print(round(Q, 1))
print(round(Q, 1))

traps: Do not say a cold cup warming on its own violates the first law. It violates the second law; the energy balance is perfect.
Do not call a PMM-2 a first-law violator. A PMM-2 passes the first law and fails the second. A PMM-1 fails the first law.
Do not say heat can never become work. In a cycle, heat cannot become work completely; some heat must be rejected. A single non-cyclic process can convert heat to work.
Do not treat kJ of work and kJ of heat as equally useful. The first law counts both; the second law ranks them.

quiz.q: State any three limitations of the first law of thermodynamics.
quiz.a: No direction; no quality difference between heat and work; it accepts a PMM-2; it gives no equilibrium or spontaneity criterion; it does not separate reversible from irreversible processes.

quiz.q: Why does the first law allow a cold cup in a warm room to warm on its own, even though it never happens?
quiz.a: The same joules can be written as room to cup. The energy balance closes. Direction is a second-law matter.

quiz.q: 0.5 kg of water cools from 90 °C to 30 °C. Take c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K. Find the heat rejected.
An inventor claims a cyclic engine takes 100 kJ heat from one reservoir and delivers 100 kJ work. Check it against the first law and the second law.
quiz.a: First law: Q = W = 100 kJ, so it passes. It is a PMM-2. The second law forbids a cyclic engine with no cold reservoir and 100 percent efficiency.

quiz.q: Define a perpetual motion machine of the second kind.
quiz.a: A hypothetical cyclic device that converts all heat from one reservoir into work, with no other effect and no cold reservoir.

quiz.q: Why are a joule of work and a joule of heat not equal in quality?
quiz.a: Work can become heat completely by friction. In a cycle, heat cannot become work completely; some heat must be rejected. Work is high-grade, low-temperature heat is low-grade.

quiz.q: A slow reversible expansion and a fast irreversible expansion of the same gas have the same start and end states. Both obey the first law. What does the first law fail to tell you?
quiz.a: It fails to separate reversible from irreversible. It gives no entropy change or lost work. The irreversible path destroys work potential; second law and exergy tell this.

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant design, exergy analysis ranks losses that the first law hides. A steam turbine with a perfect energy balance can still waste work potential. Pinch analysis uses the same second-law thinking to cut fuel in process plants. Search next for second law efficiency, exergy destruction, and PMM-2.
